_説明: English explanations shown when you click a word in code while reading in English. Same keys as glossary.json. A first line "Origin: ..." is shown folded in the speech bubble. Words missing here fall back to the Japanese glossary.json.
$ sudo:
Origin: short for superuser do (run as the administrator).
Runs the following command with administrator rights. Needed to change system settings or install software.
It asks for your password the first time (nothing appears on screen as you type).
$ apt:
Origin: short for Advanced Package Tool.
The command that manages software on Ubuntu. It installs and removes software.
$ apt install:
Installs software from the internet.
Example: sudo apt install pipx installs pipx.
$ ls:
Origin: short for list.
Shows a list of files and folders.
$ cd:
Origin: short for change directory.
Moves to another folder in the terminal.
$ cat:
Origin: short for concatenate (join together).
Shows the contents of a file.
$ ssh:
Origin: short for Secure Shell.
Logs in to a computer across the network. git also uses it to talk to GitHub.
$ ssh -T:
Origin: -T means "do not use a terminal".
Does not log in; only checks that you can connect. ssh -T git@github.com tells you whether GitHub accepts your key.
$ ssh -vT:
Origin: -v is short for verbose (in detail).
Runs ssh -T while showing in detail what happens along the way. You can see which keys were tried and where you were refused.
$ ssh -A:
Origin: -A stands for agent forwarding.
Lets the machine you logged in to use the keys in your own PC's ssh-agent. The private key is not copied. Use it only on machines you manage yourself.
$ ssh git@github.com: GitHub's SSH entrance. The username is git for everyone; which account you are is decided by your key.
$ ssh git@github-collar: Connects using the nickname github-collar set in ~/.ssh/config (connects to github.com with the chosen key).
$ ssh-keygen:
Origin: short for key generator.
Makes an SSH key (a pair of a private key and a public key). It can also delete the stored key of a host you connected to (-R), among other things.
$ ssh-keygen -t:
Origin: -t is short for type.
Chooses the type of key. ed25519 is recommended today.
$ ssh-keygen ed25519: One type of key. Short, secure and recommended today. The files are id_ed25519 (private key) and id_ed25519.pub (public key).
$ ssh-keygen -C:
Origin: -C is short for comment.
A note attached to the key. Use a name that tells you which machine's key it is. It goes at the end of the public key.
$ ssh-keygen -f:
Origin: -f is short for file.
The name and location of the key file. Without it, the key is ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.
$ ssh-keygen -N:
Origin: -N stands for new passphrase.
Sets the passphrase. -N "" makes it empty (you are not asked).
$ ssh-keygen -R:
Origin: -R is short for remove.
Deletes the old record of that host's key from ~/.ssh/known_hosts. Use it when the other machine's OS has been reinstalled.
$ ssh-add: Adds a key to ssh-agent (the helper that remembers keys). Once added, you do not have to type the passphrase every time.
$ ssh-add -l:
Origin: -l is short for list.
Shows the list of keys ssh-agent remembers.
$ ssh-copy-id:
Origin: copy id means "copy my key (ID)".
Adds your public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the other machine. From then on, you can ssh in without a password.
$ ~/.ssh: The folder for SSH keys and settings. It holds id_ed25519 (private key), id_ed25519.pub (public key), known_hosts (records of hosts you connected to), config (settings), authorized_keys (public keys allowed to log in) and so on.
$ ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub: The public key file. Register its one line of contents with GitHub. Fine to share.
$ ~/.ssh/config: The ssh settings file. For each host you connect to, you can write which key to use and a nickname.
$ ~/.ssh/collar_deploy: A key (private key) made with a name given by ssh-keygen -f. The one ending in .pub is the public key.
$ ~/.ssh/collar_deploy.pub: The public key of the key made with a name given by ssh-keygen -f. Register it under Deploy keys in the GitHub repository.
$ hostname: Shows this machine's name. Add .local after it, and machines on the same LAN can connect using that name.
$ hostname -I:
Origin: -I stands for IP address.
Shows this machine's IP address.
$ openssh-server: An ssh server. Once installed, other machines can log in to this machine with ssh.
$ exit: When you are logged in with ssh, logs out and returns to the original machine.
$ pi@raspberrypi.local:
The form "username@computer-name". Connects to raspberrypi.local as the user pi.
With scp, write the destination path after the : that follows.
$ nano: A text editor used inside the terminal. Ctrl + O saves, Ctrl + X quits.
$ git: Software that records changes to source code. It keeps track of when and what changed, lets you go back to an earlier state, and lets you put code on GitHub.
$ git clone: Downloads a whole repository (a complete set of source code) from the internet.
$ git init:
Origin: init is short for initialize.
Makes the current folder managed by git. A hidden folder called .git is created inside. Only once per project, at the start.
$ git add: Picks the changes to go into the next commit.
. means "the current folder".
Puts every change in the current folder into the next commit (except what is listed in .gitignore).
$ git commit:
Origin: commit means to fix something in place, to put it on record.
Saves the changes picked with git add as one record (a commit). You can go back to this state later.
$ git commit -m:
Origin: -m is short for message.
Write the commit description inside quotes ("). Example: git commit -m "Add I2C reading"
$ git push: Sends (uploads) your local commits to GitHub.
$ git push --tags: Also sends the markers made with git tag to GitHub. git push alone does not send them.
$ git pull: Brings new commits on GitHub into your local repository. Used to get changes made on another PC.
$ git diff:
Origin: diff is short for difference.
Shows uncommitted changes line by line. - is a removed line, + is an added line.
$ git restore: Returns a file to its last committed state. Uncommitted changes are lost and cannot be recovered.
$ git tag:
Origin: a tag is a label, like one tied to luggage.
Puts a named marker such as v1.0.0 on the current commit. Lets you find and take out a version you shipped later.
$ git --version: Shows git's version. If it shows one, git is installed.
$ git config:
Origin: config is short for configuration.
Makes or shows git settings.
$ git config --global: Makes the setting apply to all repositories of this user on this PC. It is written to ~/.gitconfig. Without it, the setting applies only to the current repository.
$ git --list: Shows a list of the settings.
$ git user.name: The name recorded in commits.
$ git user.email: The email address recorded in commits. Once on GitHub, anyone who looks at the commits can see it. If you do not want to show it, use the noreply address shown under GitHub's Settings → Emails.
$ git init.defaultBranch: The name of the first branch of repositories made with git init. Make it main, the same as GitHub.
$ git pull.rebase:
Origin: rebase means "to change the base".
How git pull combines things when both sides changed. false means merge (adds one record that combines them).
$ git pull.rebase false: When both sides changed, git pull combines them with a merge. It is easy to see what happened, so start with this.
$ git core.editor: The editor that opens when you write a commit description and so on. With nano, Ctrl + O → Enter saves, and Ctrl + X closes.
$ git status: Shows the list of changed files, staged files and new files, and whether you are ahead of GitHub. When in doubt, start with this.
$ git diff --staged:
Origin: staged means "put on the stage".
Shows the changes put on the stage with git add (what goes into the next commit).
$ git log:
Origin: a log is a record or diary.
Shows the commit history, newest first. Quit with q.
$ git log --oneline: Shows each commit on one line, with just its number (first 7 characters) and description.
$ git log -p:
Origin: -p is short for patch (the difference made by a change).
Also shows what each commit changed. Add a file name to see only that file.
$ git show: With a commit number, shows that commit's description and what it changed.
$ git remote: Works with remotes (repositories somewhere else, such as GitHub).
$ git remote -v:
Origin: -v is short for verbose (in detail).
Shows the names and URLs of the registered remotes.
$ git remote add: Registers a remote with a name. git remote add origin URL registers the URL under the name origin.
$ git remote set-url: Changes the URL of a registered remote. For example, when switching from HTTPS to SSH.
$ git origin: The name of a remote. By convention, the GitHub repository is called origin. When you clone, it gets this name automatically.
$ git lan: A remote name (one you chose yourself). In Chapter 8, the storage (bare repository) made on a PC on the same LAN.
$ git main: The name of the main branch. New repositories made on GitHub use main.
$ git master: The name of the main branch used in older repositories. Today, main is normal.
$ git push -u:
Origin: -u is short for upstream (where the branch connects to).
Makes git remember where this branch connects. After that, git push and git pull alone are enough. Add it only the first time.
$ git --delete: git push origin --delete name deletes a branch on GitHub.
$ git switch: Switches branches. The files in the working folder change to that branch's state.
$ git switch -c:
Origin: -c is short for create.
Makes a new branch and moves to it.
$ git switch --detach:
Origin: detach means to separate.
Leaves the branch and moves to the state of a commit number or tag. Use it just for looking; to go back, git switch main.
$ git branch: Shows the list of branches. The one with * is the branch you are on.
$ git branch -d:
Origin: -d is short for delete.
Deletes a branch. Branches that have not been merged are not deleted (so you do not lose important changes).
$ git branch -D: Forcibly deletes even branches that have not been merged. Commits that existed only on that branch can no longer be seen.
$ git branch -m:
Origin: -m is short for move (here, rename).
Renames a branch. git branch -m master main renames master to main.
$ git merge:
Origin: merge means to join together, like roads.
Brings the changes of the named branch into the branch you are on.
$ git merge --abort:
Origin: abort means to stop partway.
Stops a merge that has conflicts and returns to the state before it.
$ git restore --staged: Takes something off the stage. The changes to the file stay as they are.
$ git restore --source: Takes out a file as it was in the given commit and replaces the current file with it.
$ git commit --amend:
Origin: amend means to correct.
Remakes the last commit (fix its description or add something you forgot). Do not use it after pushing.
$ git --no-edit: Keeps the commit description as it is.
$ git revert:
Origin: revert means to go back.
Makes a new commit that cancels the changes of the given commit. The history is not erased, so you can use it even after pushing.
$ git stash:
Origin: stash means to put something away for later.
Sets aside uncommitted changes for a while and returns to the state of the last commit.
$ git stash pop: Brings the changes set aside with git stash back into the working folder.
$ git rm:
Origin: rm is short for remove.
Deletes a file and puts that deletion into the next commit.
$ git rm --cached:
Origin: cached means "in git's copy".
Removes the file only from git's record. The file on your PC is not deleted. Use it for files you recorded before writing them in .gitignore.
$ git rm -r:
Origin: -r is short for recursive (everything inside, too).
Applies to everything inside the folder.
$ git --cached: Removes the file only from git's record. The file on your PC is not deleted.
$ git clone --bare:
Origin: bare means exposed, with nothing around it.
Copies it as a repository with only the record and no working folder. Used as storage that other machines push to (the same form as the ones inside GitHub).
$ git --allow-unrelated-histories: Allows combining two repositories that started separately. Used when connecting to a repository made on GitHub with a README.
$ git -m:
Origin: -m is short for message.
Write the commit description inside quotes (").
$ git reset: Returns commits or the stage to an earlier state. Depending on how it is used, records can be erased, so until you understand it, use git restore or git revert.
$ git reset --hard: Forcibly returns both the working folder and the stage to the given commit's state. Uncommitted changes are lost and cannot be recovered. Do not use it.
$ git push --force: Overwrites GitHub's record with your local record. Commits that existed only on GitHub are lost. Do not use it.
$ git try-sleep: An example branch name (a branch for trying sleep mode). You can freely name branches with letters, digits and -.
$ &&:
If the previous command succeeded, runs the next one.
git add . && git commit -m "…" is the same as typing the two in order.
$ gh:
Origin: short for GitHub.
GitHub CLI. The official command for working with GitHub from the terminal. The first time, log in to GitHub with gh auth login.
$ gh repo:
Origin: repo is short for repository (where source code is kept).
Works with GitHub repositories.
$ gh repo create: Makes a new repository on GitHub.
$ gh --private: Makes a repository that only you (and people you invite) can see. To let anyone see it, use --public.
Makes the repository from the current folder (.).
$ gh --push: After making the repository, sends the current folder's commits to GitHub.
$ gh auth:
Origin: auth is short for authentication (checking that you are who you say you are).
Handles gh's login to GitHub.
$ gh auth login: Logs in to GitHub. You choose SSH or HTTPS for git operations, and with SSH it can even register your public key.
$ gh auth status: Shows the account you are logged in with and the method used for git operations (ssh or https).
$ gh config:
Origin: config is short for configuration.
Makes gh settings.
$ gh config set: Changes a setting. Written as gh config set name value.
$ gh git_protocol:
Origin: a protocol is a way of communicating.
Whether repositories made or cloned with gh use ssh or https URLs.
$ gh git_protocol ssh: Uses SSH URLs (git@github.com:…). For when your SSH key is registered with GitHub.
$ gh repo view: Shows the repository's description and README.
$ gh repo clone: Clones a GitHub repository. For your own repository, the name alone is enough, without the username.
$ collar: The project name used in this textbook's examples (a program for a cow collar). Replace it with the name of your own project.
$ code:
The command that starts VS Code from the terminal.
code collar opens the collar folder in VS Code. code . opens the current folder.
$ .gitignore: A file listing the files git should not record. One per line: folders like build/, or patterns like *.csv. Everything after # is a note.
Opens the current folder in VS Code.
$ code --install-extension: Installs a VS Code extension by its name (ID).
$ mhutchie.git-graph: The name (ID) of the "Git Graph" extension. Shows the commit history as a branching diagram.
$ github.vscode-github-actions: The name (ID) of the "GitHub Actions" extension. Shows the results of automatic builds on GitHub in VS Code.
$ eamodio.gitlens: The name (ID) of the "GitLens" extension. Shows, for each line, who changed it, when and in which commit.
$ github.vscode-pull-request-github: The name (ID) of the "GitHub Pull Requests" extension. Handles Pull Requests and Issues inside VS Code.
$ ms-vscode-remote.remote-ssh: The name (ID) of the "Remote - SSH" extension. Opens folders on a machine you connect to with ssh (Raspberry Pi, Jetson) in VS Code on your PC.
$ git --soft: git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes only the last commit. The changes stay on the stage (the same as VS Code's Undo Last Commit).
$ git HEAD~1: HEAD is the commit you are on, and ~1 means one before it. HEAD~1 means "the commit just before the current one".
$ apt update: Refreshes the list of software (which versions are available). Do it before apt install
$ ls -l: Lists files in detail (permissions, size, date and time)
Loads a settings file into the current terminal (the same as source)
